title: What About When Effort Doesn’t Work?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. takes up the hard case where students have been taught good learning strategies and still fail despite real effort. His starting point is that students will only invest effort if they believe it will pay off, so a failed attempt can quietly erode that belief. He offers a short protocol: normalize the failure, debrief individually with a student using an index card of next-time strategies, and run a Think-Pair-Share debrief when the whole class struggled. He closes with a warning against telling students to try harder, which leaves most of them with high challenge and no support. The post is a practical piece on responding to setbacks in a way that protects student motivation.
points: Students keep trying only if they believe effort pays off, so failure despite effort threatens the belief that sustains learning.
Normalizing failure signals that the teacher knows what to do next, which steadies the student.
A fifteen-minute individual debrief about how the student actually prepared, ending with an index card of strategies to try, turns failure into a plan.
For class-wide failures, a structured Think-Pair-Share debrief gets everyone reflecting on their own preparation.
Telling students to just try harder is vague advice that leaves them frustrated rather than supported.
quotes: For our students to bring effort to the mastery work in our classes, they’ve got to believe that their effort is actually going to pay off. You and I are not so different. Why try if it won’t matter?
Normalize the failure. “Yeah, this happens. I’ve seen this before. The best thing for us to do is to sit down and look at how you studied so that we can make a plan for next time.

If the failure-despite-effort is just happening with a student or two, then I like to schedule fifteen minutes with that student to look at what kind of effort they put in. I ask lots of questions here. I ask them to show me their notes.

I keep an index card between us, and we write down things to try next time on the card (e.g., “Space the three hours of studying out over two weeks in 30-minute sessions rather than doing one giant cram at the end,” or, “Quiz yourself with flashcards of key terms instead of rereading your notes”).
If it’s a whole-class failure-despite-effort, then do the debrief with the whole class. Use Think-Pair-Share to have students write what specifically they did to prepare for the thing.

Never communicate, explicitly or otherwise, “Well, you should just try harder.” This is a vague notion that, in my observations, works for about 1% of the population. For 99% of us, high challenge and no support means long-term frustration, not long-term flourishing.
